176.title: The city of nine gates (5.13–5.21)
176.hook: the Gita calls your body a city with nine gates, and asks who lives inside
176.howItsDone: In meditation many Hindus draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13, and some traditions of yoga practice closing the senses one by one to rest in the self within.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: two paths, renunciation and action, and a lotus leaf that lives in the water without getting wet. Your line was both work. Day one hundred seventy-six.
screen: `TWO PATHS — BOTH WORK.`

segments.voice: Picture an old walled city at night. Nine gates in the wall. Through every gate, all day long, traffic: carts, voices, smells from the market, news, noise. And somewhere in the middle, in a quiet courtyard, someone is sitting, perfectly at ease, watching it all come and go. Not running the gates. Not chasing the carts. Just seated. The Gita says that city is you. Count the gates on your own face and body and you'll find them. Today, chapter five, verse thirteen: who sits in the middle of the city?
screen: `AN OLD CITY, NINE GATES.` → `TRAFFIC ALL DAY LONG.` → `SOMEONE SEATED IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: having let go of all actions in the mind, the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor making anything act. The nine gates are the openings of the body: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. Everything the world sends you comes through one of them. The image is older than the Gita; the Upanishads also speak of the body as a city with gates. And in Sanskrit there's an old word-play: purusha, the person, heard as the one who dwells in the city, the pura. Now the point. Who's doing all the seeing and hearing and eating? The next verses say the Lord doesn't create our sense of being the doer, or our actions, or their fruits. That's nature, doing what nature does. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and so beings get confused. But when knowledge clears the ignorance, it lights up the highest, the way the sun lights up everything. And then a verse about how the wise see. They look with the same eye, verse eighteen says, at a learned and gentle priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns. Same eye, because the same one is seated in every city. The chapter ends this stretch plainly: the one not attached to outside contacts finds happiness within. That's the word today, the city of nine gates. Busy gates. A quiet center.
screen: `NINE GATES: EYES, EARS, NOSTRILS, MOUTH…` · `NATURE DOES THE DOING.` · `THE SAME EYE ON EVERY BEING.` · `HAPPINESS WITHIN.` · then, large: `BUSY GATES. A QUIET CENTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and visit the gates one at a time. Your eyes: notice light, even with them closed. Your ears: the nearest sound, then the farthest. Your nostrils: the cool air coming in. Your mouth: the taste that's there right now. You don't have to close any gate. Just notice the traffic, and notice that something in the middle is noticing. Rest there, seated within. The bell holds the time.
The city of nine gates. The body, with its nine openings to the world, and the self seated at ease in the middle, watching.
screen: `THE CITY OF NINE GATES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seated within. Today, when the traffic gets loud, the phone, the noise, the news, remember the courtyard, and take one breath there. Day one hundred seventy-six.

177.title: The sage's peace (5.22–5.29)
177.hook: every pleasure that comes from outside has a beginning and an end; chapter five ends with the one that doesn't
177.howItsDone: Many Hindu prayers and readings close with 'om shanti shanti shanti', a threefold wish for peace, and many practitioners use steady, even breathing like that of Gita 5.27–28 to settle before meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the city of nine gates, busy gates and a quiet center. Your line was seated within. Did you find the courtyard once, in the noise? Day one hundred seventy-seven, the end of chapter five.
screen: `THE CITY OF NINE GATES — SEATED WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Think of the best thing you ate last month. Really think about it. Now: where is it? Gone. It was wonderful, and it was over by the end of the plate. The new phone, the great weekend, the compliment that made your whole Tuesday. Each one arrived, glowed, and left, and sometimes left a little ache where it had been. Nobody in the Gita says those things are bad. But the last verses of chapter five ask a sharp question about them. Where's the happiness that doesn't have an end?
screen: `THE BEST THING YOU ATE LAST MONTH.` → `WHERE IS IT NOW?` → `A HAPPINESS WITH NO END?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: the pleasures born of contact, of the senses touching their objects, are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, and the wise don't take their delight in them. It's a strong image. A womb is where something grows. Every pleasure that depends on something outside carries, inside it, the sorrow of its ending. Then verse twenty-three sets a very practical test. Whoever can bear the rush of desire and anger here, in this life, before leaving the body, is a yogi, a happy person. Not someone who never feels desire or anger. Someone who can bear the push of it. Verse twenty-four gives the other direction: happy within, delighting within, lit from within. That person, the text says, reaches brahma-nirvana, the stillness of Brahman. Yes, nirvana: the word is in the Gita too, a blowing out. Then two verses sketch a meditation, as a preview of chapter six: shut out outside contacts, fix the gaze between the brows, even out the breath moving in and out of the nostrils. And the chapter's last verse names what's at the end of all of it. The one who knows Krishna as the one who receives every offering, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, reaches peace. Shanti. The friend of all beings. That's where the sage's peace comes from: not from getting enough, but from being held.
screen: `WOMBS OF SORROW.` · `BEAR THE PUSH OF DESIRE AND ANGER.` · `LIT FROM WITHIN.` · `THE FRIEND OF ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `SHANTI. PEACE.`

segments.voice: Verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight give a sitting, so let's borrow a gentle version. Sit tall. Let your eyes close, or rest your gaze softly, not on anything outside. Now even out the breath: in for four, out for four, the air moving quietly through the nostrils. If a want or an irritation pushes in, don't fight it. Bear it for one breath, and let it pass. Stay lit from within. The bell holds the time.
The sage's peace. Not the pleasure that begins and ends, but the peace, shanti, of the one who knows the friend of all beings.
screen: `THE SAGE'S PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: peace. Today, when a pleasure ends, a meal, a show, a good conversation, notice the little ache, and then notice what's still here. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: Lift yourself by yourself (6.1–6.9)
178.hook: the verse that says you are your own best friend, and your own worst enemy
178.howItsDone: Gita 6.5 is one of the most memorized verses of the Gita; many Hindus learn it by heart and recite it as encouragement in hard times.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of chapter five: the sage's peace, from the friend of all beings. Your line was peace. Today, chapter six, the chapter of meditation, and a friend much closer to home. Day one hundred seventy-eight.
screen: `THE SAGE'S PEACE — PEACE.`

segments.voice: Listen to the voice in your head for a minute after something goes wrong. You dropped the ball at work. You snapped at someone you love. What does the voice say? For a lot of people it says things they would never say to a friend. You always do this. What's wrong with you. If a stranger talked to you like that, you'd walk away. But this voice comes along everywhere. Chapter six of the Gita opens with two lines that millions of people know by heart, and they're about exactly this voice.
screen: `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `WHAT DOES THE VOICE SAY?` → `WORDS YOU'D NEVER SAY TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: First, Krishna clears something up. The true renouncer, verse one says, isn't the one who stops lighting the sacred fire or stops doing any work. It's the one who does what needs doing without leaning on the fruit. Then verse three: for someone climbing toward yoga, action is the way up. For someone who has arrived, stillness is the way. And then verses five and six. Lift yourself by yourself; don't let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. In Sanskrit the same word, atman, the self, comes again and again, like a mirror facing a mirror. The word for friend is bandhu: a friend, and also family, the one bound to you. Verse six explains how the same self can be both. For the one who has mastered themselves, the self is a friend. For the one who hasn't, the self behaves like an enemy. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say wait for someone to rescue you. It doesn't say you're on your own, either; the Gita is full of grace. It says the hand that lifts you starts with your own. The chapter then paints the one who has done it: steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, praise and blame. A lump of earth, a stone and gold look alike to them. And they're even-minded toward friend and foe, the good and the bad. That's today's word. Lift yourself by yourself. Be your own friend.
screen: `THE TRUE RENOUNCER STILL ACTS.` · `LIFT YOURSELF BY YOURSELF.` · `THE SELF: FRIEND OR ENEMY.` · `EARTH, STONE AND GOLD ALIKE.` · then, large: `BE YOUR OWN FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of the last time the inner voice was harsh with you. Let the words come up. Now imagine a good friend heard those words said about you. What would the friend say back? Let that answer come up, in a warm voice. Breathe with it. On each in-breath, lift, just a little, the way you'd lift someone off the floor. On each out-breath, let yourself be held. The bell holds the time.
Lift yourself by yourself. Gita six, five: the self is the friend of the self, and the enemy of the self. The lifting starts with your own hand.
screen: `LIFT YOURSELF BY YOURSELF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: your own friend. Today, once, catch the harsh voice, and answer it the way a friend would. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: How to sit (6.10–6.17)
179.hook: the Gita's own meditation instructions: the place, the seat, the spine, and how much to eat
179.tomorrow: The lamp in a windless place (6.18–6.28)
179.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a clean corner or home shrine for daily sitting, often on a mat or cloth, with a straight spine and a steady gaze, following the pattern of Gita 6.10–6.17.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: lift yourself by yourself. Your line was your own friend. Did you answer the harsh voice the way a friend would? Day one hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `LIFT YOURSELF BY YOURSELF — YOUR OWN FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Search for how to meditate and you'll get ten thousand answers. Apps, retreats, cushions that cost more than a chair. It's easy to forget that people were writing down instructions for this a very long time ago. Chapter six of the Gita has them. Not vague ones, either. Where to sit. What to sit on. How high. How to hold your head. Where to put your eyes. And then a line that surprises people: how much to eat and sleep. Today, the Gita's own instructions for sitting, verse by verse.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND ANSWERS.` → `WRITTEN DOWN LONG AGO.` → `WHERE, WHAT, HOW HIGH.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with the place. The yogi should sit alone, somewhere apart, with body and mind under control, not wanting anything, not grasping. Verse eleven: in a clean place, set a firm seat, not too high and not too low. In the old instructions it's layered: sacred kusha grass, then a deerskin, then cloth. For most people now, a folded blanket or a steady chair. The point is firm, clean, and yours. Verse twelve: sitting there, make the mind one-pointed, rein in thoughts and senses, and practice yoga to purify yourself. Verse thirteen, the posture: hold the body, head and neck in a straight line, still and steady. Gaze toward the tip of the nose, the text says, and don't look around in every direction. Verse fourteen, the heart of it: calm, without fear, the mind held, sitting with the mind on Krishna, intent on him. And then the balance. Yoga, verse sixteen says, is not for someone who eats too much, or not at all. Not for someone who sleeps too much, or stays awake too long. Verse seventeen: for the one who is moderate in food and rest, in effort, in sleeping and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow. That's it. No extremes. Not the heroic all-night vigil, not the lazy slump. The middle. That's today's word: how to sit. A clean place, a steady seat, a straight spine, a quiet gaze, and a life that isn't at war with itself.
screen: `A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.` · `BODY, HEAD, NECK IN A LINE.` · `A STILL, INWARD GAZE.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · then, large: `YOGA DESTROYS SORROW.`

segments.voice: Let's follow the verses. Find the steadiest seat near you, a chair or the floor, not too high and not too low. Sit so your body, head and neck line up, as if a thread lifts the top of your head. Let the eyes lower and soften toward the tip of the nose, or close them. Stop looking around. Now just stay still. If you pray, you can hold Krishna in mind, as verse fourteen says; if not, hold the stillness itself. The bell holds the time.
How to sit. The Gita's instructions: a clean place, a firm seat, body and head and neck in a line, a steady gaze, and moderation in food and sleep.
screen: `HOW TO SIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the posture, the place. Pick one spot in your home to be your clean, steady seat, and sit there once today, even for a minute. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: The lamp in a windless place (6.18–6.28)
180.word: The lamp in a windless place
180.hook: the Gita's picture of a settled mind is a flame that doesn't flicker
180.tomorrow: "The mind is restless" — Arjuna admits it (6.29–6.36)
180.howItsDone: Many Hindus light a lamp (diya) at the home shrine morning or evening, and some meditate by gazing at a steady flame; Gita 6.19's windless lamp is a classic image of the settled mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: how to sit. A clean place, a firm seat, a straight spine. Your line was the posture, the place. Did you find your spot? Today, what happens once you're sitting there. Day one hundred eighty.
screen: `HOW TO SIT — THE POSTURE, THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: Light a small oil lamp, a diya, near an open window, and watch it. The flame bends, leans, jumps, nearly goes out, flares back. Every breath of air pushes it around. Now carry it into an inner room and shut the door. The flame straightens. It stands up tall and still, so still it almost looks painted. Same lamp. Same oil. The only difference is the wind. Many Hindu homes light a lamp like this every evening. The Gita, chapter six, uses that exact picture for the mind.
screen: `A LAMP BY AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `SHUT THE DOOR.` → `THE FLAME STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Verse nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, that is the picture of the yogi whose mind is held, practicing union with the self. The Sanskrit is simple: dipa, the lamp; nivata, where there's no wind. Notice the lamp is still burning. A settled mind isn't a mind that's gone out. It's fully lit, just not being pushed around. Then the verses describe what that stillness opens onto. Where the mind comes to rest, seeing the self by the self, a person is content in the self. They know a joy beyond the senses, grasped by understanding, and once they're settled there they don't move from the truth. Having gained it, they count no other gain greater. Established in it, even heavy sorrow doesn't shake them. And then a definition I like a lot, from verse twenty-three: yoga is the unhooking from union with sorrow. Most people think of yoga as joining. Here it's also an unjoining: coming apart from the grip of pain. Now the practical part. Verse twenty-five: little by little, slowly, slowly, let the mind grow still. Shanaih shanaih: slowly, slowly. And verse twenty-six gives the whole method in one sentence. Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, draw it back from there and bring it under the self. That's it. Not never wandering. Coming back. Every time the wind moves the flame, you shut the door again. That's the word today: the lamp in a windless place.
screen: `A LAMP THAT DOES NOT FLICKER.` · `STILL, AND FULLY LIT.` · `UNHOOKED FROM SORROW.` · `SLOWLY, SLOWLY. COME BACK.` · then, large: `THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture a small flame in the middle of your chest, or just in front of your closed eyes. Let it burn. Each time a thought blows in, notice the flame lean. Then, gently, shut the door and watch it straighten again. Don't be annoyed at the wind. Verse twenty-six expects it. The practice is the returning, slowly, slowly, as many times as it takes. The bell holds the time.
The lamp in a windless place. Gita six, nineteen: the settled mind is a flame that burns fully and doesn't flicker.
screen: `THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: flame unwavering. Today, when your attention gets blown around, don't scold it. Shut the door and bring it back, slowly, slowly. Day one hundred eighty.

181.title: "The mind is restless" — Arjuna admits it (6.29–6.36)
181.hook: after all the instructions, Arjuna says what everyone is thinking: this is impossible
181.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often pair abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (detachment) as the two supports of meditation; the Yoga Sutra names the same pair, and many practitioners return to Gita 6.34–35 when meditation feels impossible.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lamp in a windless place. Your line was flame unwavering. How many times did you bring your attention back? If the answer is a lot, today's reading is for you. Day one hundred eighty-one.
screen: `THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE — FLAME UNWAVERING.`

segments.voice: You sit down to be still. Ten seconds in, you're thinking about lunch. Then an email. Then a conversation from 2014 that you lost, and how you should have answered. Then lunch again. If that's you, you're in very good company. Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the self in every being and the lamp that doesn't flicker. And Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age, a man who can hit a bird's eye with an arrow, stops him and says, basically: I can't do this. My mind won't hold still.
screen: `TEN SECONDS IN: LUNCH.` → `THEN A CONVERSATION FROM 2014.` → `ARJUNA: I CAN'T DO THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the vision that sets Arjuna off. The yogi, verse twenty-nine says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. And the highest yogi, verse thirty-two, is the one who looks at another's joy or pain as if it were their own. Beautiful. And Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you describe, I don't see how it can last, because the mind is restless. Then verse thirty-four, maybe the most honest line in the Gita: the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn. To hold it, I think, is as hard as holding the wind. And Krishna doesn't argue. That's the surprise. He says: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold. He agrees. Then he gives two words. By abhyasa and by vairagya, it can be held. Abhyasa: practice, doing it again and again. Vairagya: detachment, the fading of the pull, not letting every passing want drag you off. You need both. Practice alone becomes grim effort against a mind that keeps being yanked away. Detachment alone never builds the habit. Together they work like two oars. Verse thirty-six closes it: yoga is hard for the one who doesn't hold themselves, but for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. That's today's word, the mind is restless. True. And not the end of the story.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.` · `AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `KRISHNA AGREES.` · `PRACTICE AND DETACHMENT.` · then, large: `TWO OARS.`

segments.voice: Two oars, for two minutes. Sit, and pick one thing to rest on: the breath at the nose. That's the practice: coming back to it. When the mind runs off, and it will, notice where it ran. Don't chase the thought or argue with it. Just let the pull fade a little, and come back. Pull on both oars: return, and let go. Return, and let go. The bell holds the time.
The mind is restless. Arjuna's honest complaint, Gita six, thirty-four. Krishna agrees, and answers: by practice and detachment it can be held.
screen: `"THE MIND IS RESTLESS" — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: practice and detachment. Today, when your mind runs off, don't take it as failure. Take it as one more stroke of the oar. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: The one who fell short (6.37–6.47)
182.hook: Arjuna asks the question under every new habit: what if I start, and fail?
182.howItsDone: Gita 6.40 is often quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who have lapsed in practice; many readers divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and chapter six closes the first.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna admitted it: the mind is restless. Krishna agreed, and gave two oars. Your line was practice and detachment. Day one hundred eighty-two, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.
screen: `"THE MIND IS RESTLESS" — PRACTICE AND DETACHMENT.`

segments.voice: Look at this week. The city of nine gates, seated within. The sage's peace. Lift yourself by yourself, your own friend. How to sit. The lamp in a windless place. And the restless mind. That's a lot to live up to. So Arjuna asks the question anyone asks on day three of a new habit. What about the person who starts with real faith, but can't keep it up? The mind wanders off, and they never get there. Do they lose both worlds? Are they like a small cloud, torn off from the big one, that just thins out and disappears?
screen: `A WEEK TO LIVE UP TO.` → `WHAT IF I START, AND FAIL?` → `A CLOUD, TORN OFF AND GONE?`

segments.voice: It's a painful picture: the torn cloud. You left the ordinary life, you didn't reach the spiritual one, and now you're neither. Krishna's answer is one of the kindest passages in the Gita. Verse forty: there is no destruction for them, Arjuna, neither here nor in the next world. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The word he uses there, tata, is tender, the way an elder speaks to a child. Then he tells what happens. The one who fell short reaches the worlds of the good, and stays long. Then they're born again, into a good and prosperous home. Or, rarer, into a family of wise yogis. And there, verse forty-three says, they get back the understanding they had before, and they strive again, harder. Verse forty-four: they're carried forward by their earlier practice, even without meaning to be. Nothing done is wasted. Every sit, every returned thought, every day of practice counts, and it carries. Through many lifetimes of effort, the yogi comes to the goal. The chapter then ends by lifting the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritual-doers, and saying that of all yogis, the one who turns to Krishna with faith, with the inner self absorbed in him, is the closest. And with that, the first six chapters of the Gita close. Many readers see them as the part about action and the self. That's the word today, the one who fell short. And the answer: nothing is lost.
screen: `THE TORN CLOUD.` · `NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD IS LOST.` · `THEY PICK UP WHERE THEY LEFT OFF.` · `EARLIER PRACTICE CARRIES THEM.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look back over this week of practice, or this whole path so far. Think of a day you skipped, or a sit that was all wandering. Instead of counting it against yourself, picture it the way verse forty-four describes: as momentum. Every minute you did sit is still moving you. Breathe in, and feel it carrying you. Breathe out, and let the missed days go. The bell holds the time.
The one who fell short. Gita six, forty: the one who strives and doesn't arrive isn't lost. Earlier practice carries them forward.
screen: `THE ONE WHO FELL SHORT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nothing is lost. Today, pick back up one good thing you dropped, without an apology. Day one hundred eighty-two.

original.note: Sanskrit: tata, a tender address, 'my dear', used by an elder to a child; Krishna uses it in 6.40.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you quit, it didn't count.
what it means: no one who does good is lost; every bit of practice carries forward, even across lifetimes.

what a scholar hears: 6.38's 'chinnabhram iva', like a torn-off cloud, is answered in 6.40 with 'na hi kalyana-krt kaschid durgatim tata gacchati'; many commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and six closes the first.
